content.title: About
content.content: Almonds are the edible seeds of the almond tree (Prunus dulcis), which is native to the Middle East and Central Asia and is now grown in many warm regions of the world. They have a mild, slightly sweet, nutty flavor and a crunchy texture. Almonds are eaten raw, roasted, or blanched and are used in baking, desserts, spreads, and almond milk.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Almonds are related to peaches, plums, and cherries, and the almond itself is the seed inside the fruit's pit.
Sweet almonds are the ones eaten as food; bitter almonds contain compounds that are toxic when raw and are not sold as ordinary snacks.
Almond trees have been cultivated for thousands of years.
Almonds are used to make almond flour, almond butter, marzipan, and almond milk.
Almond blossoms appear in early spring, before the leaves.

items.title: Rich in vitamin E
items.content: Almonds are one of the best food sources of vitamin E, an antioxidant that helps protect cells.

items.title: Provides healthy fats
items.content: Almonds contain mostly monounsaturated fats, which can be part of a heart-friendly diet.

items.title: Contains magnesium
items.content: Magnesium supports normal muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Provides protein and fiber
items.content: Almonds contribute plant protein and fiber, which support fullness.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Almonds contain more calcium than most other nuts.

items.title: Tree nut allergy
items.content: Almonds can cause allergic reactions, which may be severe in some people.

items.title: High in calories
items.content: Almonds are calorie-dense, so portions should be moderate.

items.title: Choking hazard
items.content: Whole almonds are not suitable for young children because they can cause choking.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Almonds contain oxalates, which people prone to kidney stones may need to limit. Bitter almonds should never be eaten raw.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Almonds can be eaten as a snack, added to oatmeal, yogurt, salads, and baked goods, or ground into almond flour and almond butter. Soaking or blanching almonds softens them and makes the skins easy to remove. Unsalted or lightly salted almonds are a good option.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store almonds in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For longer storage, keep them in the refrigerator or freezer, since their oils can turn rancid. Discard almonds that smell bitter, sharp, or stale.

content.title: About
content.content: Cheese quiche, meatless is a savory tart made with a pastry crust, eggs, and creamy cheese, prepared without any meat. It offers a smooth, buttery flavor with a lightly crisp crust, suitable for vegetarians and anyone seeking a lighter alternative to traditional quiche.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Quiche originates from the Lorraine region of France, where it was historically filled with various ingredients.
Using cream cheese gives the dish a softer texture compared to classic quiche with bacon.
The meat‑free version is a staple in vegetarian menus of many restaurants and cafés.
The crust can be shortcrust or puff pastry, depending on the desired flakiness.
Quiche is easy to cut into portions, making it popular for picnics and buffets.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Cream cheese and eggs provide high‑quality protein essential for tissue repair and maintenance.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: The cheese contributes a notable amount of calcium, supporting bone and dental health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs and cheese supply B2, B12, and folate, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Lower saturated fat
items.content: Using low‑fat cheese reduces saturated fat compared with traditional meat‑filled quiche.

items.title: Contains vitamin D
items.content: Cream cheese provides a modest amount of vitamin D, aiding calcium absorption.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cream cheese may trigger allergic reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Quiche is calorie‑dense due to cheese and eggs, so portion control is advisable for weight‑managed diets.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Many cream cheeses are salted; those monitoring sodium intake should choose reduced‑salt varieties.

items.title: Risk of foodborne illness
items.content: Eggs must be fully cooked; undercooked eggs can harbor salmonella.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the quiche warm or at room temperature, sliced into individual portions. It pairs well with fresh green salads, a light mustard vinaigrette, or a simple yogurt dip.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the baked quiche to room temperature, then store it in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Reheat in the oven or microwave to restore the crust’s crispness before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Cuban crackers are crisp, thin biscuits made from wheat flour, vegetable oil, and a pinch of salt. They have a light golden color, delicate texture, and a subtle sweet‑savory flavor typical of traditional Cuban snacks.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cuban crackers first appeared in the early 20th century as a way to preserve bread in the hot climate.
They are traditionally served with cheese, avocado, or guacamole.
The original recipe includes a small amount of sugar, giving the crackers a faint sweetness.
Crackers are often used as a base for canapés at parties and buffets.
In Cuba they are commonly called “paneles.”

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Crackers provide slowly digestible carbohydrates that help sustain energy and fullness.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Unlike many snack biscuits, Cuban crackers are baked with a modest amount of oil.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Wheat flour supplies modest amounts of B1, B2, and niacin, which support metabolism.

items.title: Gentle on digestion
items.content: Their light texture makes them easy to digest, suitable as a mild snack during minor stomach upset.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: A small amount of fiber helps maintain regular bowel function.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Made from wheat flour, these crackers are not suitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Salt content
items.content: Some varieties are salted; those monitoring sodium intake should choose unsalted versions.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Because they contain simple carbs, crackers can raise blood sugar levels, which is relevant for diabetics.

items.title: Possible additives
items.content: Commercial versions may contain preservatives or flavor enhancers that some consumers prefer to avoid.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cuban crackers can be enjoyed straight from the pack, paired with cheese, ham, avocado, or guacamole, or used as a base for mini‑sandwiches. They also add a pleasant crunch when sprinkled into soups.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep crackers in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life store them in the refrigerator to prevent oil from going rancid. Discard any that develop a stale or off‑flavor.

content.title: About
content.content: Ham is smoked pork meat obtained from the hind leg of the pig. It has a rich aroma, a slightly salty taste and a firm yet tender texture. Ham is often added to vegetable dishes, salads and sandwiches.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditionally ham is smoked over wood smoke, which gives it its characteristic flavor.
Ham can be sold ready‑to‑eat or require a brief heating before consumption.
Different countries have their own versions: Spanish jamón serrano, Italian prosciutto, and American smoked ham.
Smoking extends shelf life without the need for artificial preservatives.
Ham is a staple in many cuisines for quick, hearty meals.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Ham provides high‑quality animal protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: It contains B1, B6 and B12 vitamins that support nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Iron
items.content: Ham supplies heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: Zinc
items.content: Zinc in ham contributes to immune health and wound healing.

items.title: Beneficial fats
items.content: A modest amount of monounsaturated fats in ham can be part of a heart‑healthy diet when eaten in moderation.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Ham is often salty, so people with hypertension should limit their intake.

items.title: Nitrates and preservatives
items.content: Some hams contain nitrates, which may be harmful in excessive amounts.

items.title: Pork allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to pork.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Ham is relatively calorie‑dense, so portion control is advisable, especially on weight‑loss diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice ham thinly and add it to vegetable salads, bake it together with vegetables, use it in sandwiches, or quickly sauté it for a protein‑rich stir‑fry. It is often warmed on a skillet or in the oven before serving.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store ham in the refrigerator at 0 °C–4 °C in its original packaging or an airtight container. Fresh smoked ham keeps for up to 2 weeks, while cooked ham lasts up to 1 month. Discard if it develops an off‑odor or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Ground lamb is finely minced meat from a young sheep, obtained from lean cuts of the carcass. It has a delicate, slightly sweet flavor and a tender texture typical of young meat. Ground lamb is widely used in Mediterranean, Middle Eastern and Caucasian cuisines.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Lamb grows faster than adult sheep, making its meat more tender.
In many cultures ground lamb is considered a delicacy and is often served at celebrations.
Lamb is rich in heme iron, which is highly bioavailable.
Traditional recipes often pair ground lamb with herbs such as mint, rosemary, and cumin.
Ground lamb is a common base for kebabs, meatballs, and pastry fillings.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Lamb provides complete protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Rich in vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 supports nerve function and red blood cell formation.

items.title: Source of zinc
items.content: Zinc strengthens the immune system and aids wound healing.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: The iron in lamb is easily absorbed, helping prevent anemia.

items.title: Contains omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Small amounts of omega‑3 support heart and vascular health.

items.title: High in saturated fat
items.content: Excessive intake may raise cholesterol levels.

items.title: Risk of foodborne illness
items.content: Raw ground lamb can harbor pathogenic bacteria; cook thoroughly.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to lamb.

items.title: Purine content
items.content: People with gout should limit consumption.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Ground lamb can be sautéed, braised, baked, or grilled. It is used for kebabs, meatballs, stuffed vegetables, pasta sauces, and pies. Before cooking, trim excess fat and season with herbs and spices to taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep ground lamb in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze in a freezer‑safe bag for up to 3 months. Thaw in the fridge before use, never at room temperature.
